{
  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-06",
  "sketch": {
    "components": ["Mobile app", "Notification composer service", "Device token registry", "Order service", "Lock screen notification UI"],
    "dataStores": ["Device token registry", "Order records"],
    "externalServices": ["Mobile push provider (APNs/FCM)"],
    "trustBoundaries": ["Backend to push provider", "Push provider to device OS", "Device OS to physical bystander"],
    "dataClasses": ["pii"],
    "exposure": "internal",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Anyone near a locked phone can read the customer's home address",
      "scenario": "A bystander, coworker, abusive partner or thief holding the locked device reads the notification preview without unlocking it. Because the payload carries the full order contents and delivery address, they learn where the customer lives and what they bought, with no authentication at all. On a shared desk or a stolen phone this needs zero skill.",
      "component": "Lock screen notification UI",
      "likelihood": 5,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The app sends push notifications that include the full order contents and delivery address. Notifications show on the lock screen by default." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-359", "CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "The order and home address show up on the lock screen, so anyone who can see the phone can read them without unlocking it.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Hide order details behind device unlock",
        "given": "a push notification containing order contents or a delivery address",
        "when": "the notification is delivered to a locked device",
        "then": "only a non-identifying summary (for example \"Your order has an update\") is shown, and the order contents and address are revealed only after the user unlocks the device and the app fetches them over an authenticated session"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Customer addresses sent in clear text through the push provider",
      "scenario": "Push payloads traverse Apple's and Google's infrastructure, where they are processed and may be logged or retained outside our control. Putting the full order contents and delivery address in the payload hands a copy of customer PII to a third party for every order event, and anyone with access to provider-side logs or our provider credentials can read it in bulk.",
      "component": "Notification composer service to push provider",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The app sends push notifications that include the full order contents and delivery address." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-359", "CWE-311"],
      "plainLanguage": "The notification text goes through Apple/Google servers, so their systems see every customer's address and order.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Keep PII out of push payloads",
        "given": "an order update to notify",
        "when": "the backend builds the push payload for the provider",
        "then": "the payload contains only a non-sensitive event type and an opaque order reference, and the app retrieves order contents and the delivery address from our API using the user's authenticated session"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "Spoofing",
      "title": "Stale device token delivers one customer's order to a different person",
      "scenario": "Device tokens are reassigned when a phone is sold, factory reset, restored from a backup or an app is reinstalled, and tokens linger if they are not re-bound to the logged-in user at every login and logout. The next holder of that token receives notifications containing the previous customer's order contents and delivery address on their own lock screen.",
      "component": "Device token registry",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 4,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The app sends push notifications that include the full order contents and delivery address." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-384", "CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "If a phone changes hands or the app is reinstalled, old notifications can land on the wrong person's phone.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Bind device tokens to the current session",
        "given": "a registered push token",
        "when": "a user logs out, a different user logs in, or the provider reports the token as changed or unregistered",
        "then": "the old user-to-token binding is deleted immediately and no further order notifications are sent to that token until it is re-registered by an authenticated user"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "ElevationOfPrivilege",
      "title": "Notification can be requested for someone else's order",
      "scenario": "The notification composer takes an order identifier and renders the order contents and delivery address into the message. If it does not check that the order belongs to the targeted user, an internal caller, a buggy job or a tampered event can enumerate order ids and have another customer's address delivered to an attacker-controlled device, turning the notification channel into a bulk PII read primitive.",
      "component": "Notification composer service",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 5,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "The app sends push notifications that include the full order contents and delivery address." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-639", "CWE-285"],
      "plainLanguage": "Asking for a notification about any order number could send that stranger's address to your own phone.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Verify order ownership before composing a notification",
        "given": "a request to notify a device about an order",
        "when": "the composer resolves the order contents and delivery address",
        "then": "it sends the notification only if the order's owner matches the user currently bound to the target device token, and otherwise drops the request and records the mismatch"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Order details mirrored to watches, car screens and desktop notification centres",
      "scenario": "Mobile platforms replay notifications to paired wearables, CarPlay/Android Auto displays, TV casts and mirrored desktop sessions, and keep them in notification history. A customer who screen-shares a laptop or wears a watch in a meeting exposes the full order contents and delivery address to everyone watching, because the sensitive text is in the notification itself rather than behind the app.",
      "component": "Mobile app notification content",
      "likelihood": 3,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Notifications show on the lock screen by default." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-200"],
      "plainLanguage": "Phones copy notifications to watches, cars and laptops, so the address can pop up on a screen other people are looking at.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Mark order notifications as sensitive to platform surfaces",
        "given": "an order notification",
        "when": "the platform decides whether to mirror or persist it",
        "then": "it is flagged as private/sensitive so detailed content is suppressed on mirrored and public surfaces and is not retained in notification history"
      }
    },
    {
      "stride": "InformationDisclosure",
      "title": "Default-on detailed notifications give customers no way to opt out",
      "scenario": "The design makes detailed lock screen notifications the default, so every customer, including people in shelters or shared housing who would never consent to their address appearing on a shared screen, is opted in without being asked. An attacker who shares the household simply watches the phone. There is no documented setting that lets a customer reduce the detail.",
      "component": "Notification preferences",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Notifications show on the lock screen by default." }
      ],
      "asvs": [],
      "cwe": ["CWE-1188", "CWE-359"],
      "plainLanguage": "Detailed notifications are turned on for everyone automatically, with no way for a customer to say no.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Default to minimal detail with user-controlled opt-in",
        "given": "a customer who has enabled push notifications",
        "when": "the app configures notification content",
        "then": "the default is a non-identifying summary, and showing order contents or the delivery address requires an explicit per-user opt-in that can be revoked at any time"
      }
    }
  ]
}
